segments.t: In her small Parisian apartment, Camille Valentini has a hurried breakfast with her visiting mother, Annick. While Annick comments on celebrity hairstyles and asks about Camille's relationship with Mathias, Camille tries not to be late for work. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Tu ne prends pas de petit-déjeuner?
Maman, je suis très en retard.
Assieds-toi et mange un peu.
Qui coiffe cette pauvre actrice?
Les agents ne s'occupent pas des coiffures.
Dis-moi, Mathias est gentil avec toi?
Oui, il est bien plus gentil qu'avant.
On se voit et on déjeune ensemble.
Regarde, il m'a offert une jolie lampe.
C'est facile quand on est très riche.
J'allume ta belle bougie tous les soirs.
J'aurais dû garder un enfant à la maison.
Tu as un vrai don pour le drame.
Fais bien attention sur ton vélo.
Let's examine how Annick and Camille discuss family and work over breakfast.
Tu ne prends pas de petit-déjeuner?
'Are you not having breakfast?' Literally 'little lunch', the compound meaning 'breakfast' pairs with 'take' in French rather than 'have'. After a negative, 'any' shrinks to a plain 'of'.
Maman, je suis très en retard.
'Mom, I am very late.' Literally 'in delay', this everyday expression is how you say 'late' in French, boosted here by 'very'.
Assieds-toi et mange un peu.
'Sit down and eat a little.' Annick attaches 'yourself' right onto the command with a hyphen to say 'sit down' in French, then softens 'eat' with 'a little'.
Qui coiffe cette pauvre actrice?

'Who styles this poor actress's hair?' One compact French action covers 'styles someone's hair' without needing a separate word meaning 'hair'. Before 'actress', 'poor' means 'unfortunate' rather than 'broke'.
Les agents ne s'occupent pas des coiffures.
'Agents do not deal with hairstyles.' Built from 'occupy oneself of', this handy expression means 'take care of' or 'handle', while 'agents' keeps its article even in general statements.
Dis-moi, Mathias est gentil avec toi?
'Tell me, is Mathias nice to you?' Starting with a warm 'tell me' opener, French says 'nice with you' where English says 'nice to you'.
Oui, il est bien plus gentil qu'avant.
'Yes, he is much nicer than before.' Placing 'well' in front of 'more nice' gives you 'much nicer' in French, followed by 'than before' clipped together with an apostrophe.
On se voit et on déjeune ensemble.
'We see each other and have lunch together.' Adding a reciprocal marker before 'sees' turns 'we see' into 'we see each other', paired with a single-word action meaning 'have lunch' in French.
Regarde, il m'a offert une jolie lampe.
'Look, he gave me a pretty lamp.' When talking about gifts in French, speakers say 'offered' rather than plain 'gave', tucking 'to me' right before the helper.
C'est facile quand on est très riche.
'It is easy when one is very rich.' Here casual 'one' keeps its general sense of 'people in general' rather than 'we', alongside the easy cognate 'rich'.
J'allume ta belle bougie tous les soirs.
'I light your lovely candle every evening.' Literally 'all the evenings', that closing three-word chunk is how you say 'every evening' in French, while 'light' also serves for switching on lamps.
J'aurais dû garder un enfant à la maison.
'I should have kept a child at home.' Combining 'would have' with 'had to' builds 'I should have' in French, and 'at the house' is the natural idiom meaning 'at home'.
Tu as un vrai don pour le drame.
'You have a real gift for drama.' To describe an innate talent rather than a wrapped present, French chooses a crisp three-letter word meaning 'gift' or 'knack'.
Fais bien attention sur ton vélo.

'Be very careful on your bicycle.' Literally 'make well attention', this caring send-off is what you'd say for 'be really careful', ending with the everyday clipped form of 'bicycle'. Now let's hear Camille and Annick's morning conversation again at full speed.
Tu ne prends pas de petit-déjeuner?
Maman, je suis très en retard.
Assieds-toi et mange un peu.
Qui coiffe cette pauvre actrice?
Les agents ne s'occupent pas des coiffures.
Dis-moi, Mathias est gentil avec toi?
Oui, il est bien plus gentil qu'avant.
On se voit et on déjeune ensemble.
Regarde, il m'a offert une jolie lampe.
C'est facile quand on est très riche.
J'allume ta belle bougie tous les soirs.
J'aurais dû garder un enfant à la maison.
Tu as un vrai don pour le drame.
Fais bien attention sur ton vélo.

Annick's visit reminds Camille of her complicated family situation, as Mathias remains her secret father. Despite the maternal guilt, Camille hurries out the door to face another busy day at the agency. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
